excerpt: Hit by a drunk driver on South Kings Highway (US-17 Business) through Surfside Beach? A Grand Strand DUI-crash guide to your South Carolina rights, deadlines, and the insurance pathways that actually pay.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a lawsuit after a drunk-driver crash in Surfside Beach?
faqs.answer: In South Carolina, you have three years from the crash date to file a personal-injury lawsuit under S.C. Code Ann. § 15-3-530. Wrongful-death claims (S.C. Code Ann. § 15-51-10) carry the same three years, running from the date of death under § 15-3-530(6), and are brought by the estate's personal representative (§ 15-51-20). Miss the date and the court will dismiss your case regardless of how clear the drunk driver's fault was. Narrow exceptions (minors, incapacitated plaintiffs, government defendants) can shift the timing; a claim against a government defendant generally has only two years under § 15-78-110.

faqs.question: The drunk driver fled the scene of my crash on US-17 Business. Can I still recover?
faqs.answer: Yes. Leaving an injury crash is a crime under S.C. Code Ann. § 56-5-1210 (a felony when it causes great bodily injury or death). Your own uninsured-motorist (UM) coverage under S.C. Code Ann. § 38-77-150 covers an unidentified driver if you reported the crash to police promptly and there was physical contact with the other vehicle, an independent witness who signs an affidavit, or a recording of the crash (§ 38-77-170). Cooperate with the investigation, and your UM carrier steps in as if it were the at-fault driver's insurer — subject to your limits, which a named insured or resident relative can sometimes stack from other household vehicles up to the coverage on the vehicle involved (§ 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance Co., 406 S.C. 609 (2013)).

faqs.question: The drunk driver was a tourist from out of state in a rental car. Who pays?
faqs.answer: Usually a layered combination. The driver's personal auto policy from their home state typically provides primary coverage and follows them into South Carolina; the rental company's policy may sit excess; and your own UM/UIM under S.C. Code Ann. §§ 38-77-150 and 38-77-160 fills the gap when those limits run out. Service on out-of-state defendants runs through the SC Director of Motor Vehicles under the non-resident motorist statute.

faqs.question: I had a couple of drinks too. Can I still sue the drunk driver who hit me?
faqs.answer: Probably yes, as long as you were 50% or less at fault. South Carolina follows modified comparative negligence with a 51% bar under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991). If a jury finds you 20% at fault and the drunk driver 80%, your damages drop by 20%. At 51% or higher you recover nothing — which is why the defense will push your share of fault as high as it will go.

faqs.question: Can I sue the bar or restaurant that over-served the drunk driver?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. South Carolina has no dram-shop act, but a bar or restaurant that knowingly serves an intoxicated patron violates S.C. Code Ann. §§ 61-4-580 and 61-6-2220, and courts treat that as negligence per se (Tobias v. Sports Club, Inc., 332 S.C. 90 (1998); Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill, Inc., 388 S.C. 407 (2010)). For claims arising after January 1, 2026, § 61-2-147 makes the establishment jointly and severally liable for 50% of your actual damages when the verdict also runs against a driver charged with DUI. These cases live or die on evidence — receipts, POS time stamps, surveillance video, witnesses to visible intoxication — and that evidence disappears fast without preservation letters in the first weeks.
